361.place: Klondike region and Dawson City, Yukon, Canada
361.event: Gold was found on Bonanza Creek, a tributary of the Klondike River, in August 1896, and when news reached the United States in July 1897 it set off a stampede. More than 100,000 people set out for the Klondike, but only some 30,000 to 40,000 actually reached Dawson City, many after brutal journeys over the Chilkoot and White passes. According to the US National Park Service, only a few of those who arrived obtained the wealth they had dreamed of along the way.
361.explanation: A single report of riches drew tens of thousands into hardship, and the hope of gain kept pulling new waves of people north long after the best claims had been taken.
361.tie_back: The kural calls desire the seed that unfailingly produces birth after birth, and the gold rush shows on a human scale how one seed of craving keeps generating new journeys, new hardships and new disappointments.
361._accuracy_note: The event shows craving multiplying itself in one lifetime, but the kural's claim about desire as the seed of repeated rebirth cannot be illustrated historically.

362.place: Yasnaya Polyana and Astapovo, Russian Empire (now Russia)
362.event: In his later decades Leo Tolstoy preached a life of simplicity and renunciation, while still living on his family estate at Yasnaya Polyana. On the night of 27-28 October 1910 (Old Style), aged 82, he secretly left the estate with his doctor, leaving a letter saying he was going away for good. He fell ill on the train and died of pneumonia at the small railway station of Astapovo on 7 November 1910 (20 November in the modern calendar).
362.explanation: At the end of his life Tolstoy chose to abandon home and comfort to live out the detachment he had long written about, even though he did not live to carry it through.
362.tie_back: The kural says that if one must desire anything it should be freedom itself, the desire to be free of desire, and Tolstoy's final flight was the act of a man whose one remaining wish was to leave his worldly life behind.
362._accuracy_note: The flight is well documented, but Tolstoy's precise motives were complex and are partly a matter of interpretation, including family strains.

363.event_title: Diocletian gives up the throne and retires to Split
363.place: Nicomedia (now Izmit, Turkey) and Split, Croatia (Roman Empire)
363.event: On 1 May 305 the Roman emperor Diocletian, who had ruled for more than twenty years, voluntarily abdicated, an almost unheard-of step for a Roman emperor. He retired to the great palace he had built on the Adriatic coast at what is now Split, in Croatia. Apart from a brief appearance at an imperial conference at Carnuntum in 308, he stayed in his palace for the rest of his life while rivals fought over the empire.
363.explanation: Diocletian walked away from supreme power at a time when most emperors kept it until violent death, and did not take it back while the empire's rulers fought for it.
363.tie_back: The kural ranks freedom from wanting above any treasure of this world, and Diocletian's choice of a quiet palace over the throne of the Roman world shows the highest worldly prize being let go.
363._accuracy_note: A documented renunciation of supreme power, but the sources do not establish that Diocletian acted from inner freedom from desire rather than age, illness or policy.

364.event_title: Ludwig Wittgenstein gives away his inherited fortune
364.event: Ludwig Wittgenstein, son of one of the richest industrial families in Austria-Hungary, inherited a fortune when his father died in 1913. After serving in the First World War, during which he completed the work later published as the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, he gave away his share of the family fortune. He then trained as a teacher and worked in village schools in Lower Austria in the early 1920s, living very simply.
364.explanation: One of the great philosophers of the twentieth century chose plain living over wealth as he devoted himself to questions of truth and meaning.
364.tie_back: The kural says purity is freedom from desire, and that this freedom comes from longing for truth; Wittgenstein's giving up of riches alongside his single-minded search for clarity offers a modern parallel.
364._accuracy_note: The renunciation of wealth is documented, but the sources do not tie it directly to a longing for truth, and his teaching years were troubled.

365.event_title: Queen Christina abdicates but seeks other crowns
365.event: Queen Christina of Sweden abdicated on 6 June 1654, the day her cousin Charles X Gustav was crowned, and left Sweden at once; she had secretly become a Roman Catholic and settled in Rome. Within a few years she was negotiating with Cardinal Mazarin of France in a scheme to make herself queen of Naples, which collapsed in 1657. About ten years later, with the support of Pope Clement IX, she tried without success to be chosen for the throne of Poland.
365.explanation: Christina gave up a throne in outward form, yet her later schemes show that the wish to reign had not left her.
365.tie_back: The kural says only those who have cut off desire are truly renunciants, and that others, whatever they have given up, are not free in the same way, which is precisely the contrast between Christina's abdication and her later pursuit of crowns.
365._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of outward renunciation without inner renunciation, though her reasons for abdicating were mixed and partly religious.

366.event_title: John Wesley holds his spending fixed as his income rises
366.event: As a young fellow at Oxford, John Wesley found he could live on about 28 pounds a year, and as his income rose over the following years from 30 to about 120 pounds, he kept his own expenses at that same level and gave the rest away. In his sermon The Use of Money he urged Methodists to gain all they could, save all they could and give all they could, and he warned them repeatedly about the danger of riches.
366.explanation: Wesley treated rising income not as a chance to live better but as a danger to be guarded against, and built a rule into his life to keep wanting from growing.
366.tie_back: The kural says that standing in fear of desire is itself virtue, because desire deceives, and Wesley's fixed allowance was a deliberate guard against the way more money tends to create more wants.
366._accuracy_note: Wesley's documented self-restraint fits the kural's vigilance well, though the exact yearly figures come from his own later accounts as relayed by historians.

367.event_title: Vinoba Bhave receives the first Bhoodan land gift
367.place: Pochampalli, Nalgonda district, Hyderabad State (now Telangana), India
367.event: Vinoba Bhave, a disciple of Gandhi who lived as an ascetic, was walking through Telangana in 1951 when landless Dalit families in the village of Pochampalli asked him for land. On 18 April 1951 a local landowner, Ramachandra Reddy, offered 100 acres in response to his appeal. Vinoba went on to walk across India for years asking landowners to give land to the landless, launching the Bhoodan (land-gift) movement, and in 1958 he received the first Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership.
367.explanation: A man who owned nothing and asked nothing for himself was able to persuade others to give away land on a scale no law had achieved.
367.tie_back: The kural says that when desire is cut off completely, the deeds that lead to lasting good come of their own accord, and Vinoba's desireless life became the source of a movement of giving.
367._accuracy_note: Vinoba's personal renunciation and the good it enabled fit the kural, though much of the pledged land was never distributed and the link to undying deeds is interpretive.

368.event_title: Ludwig II of Bavaria's building debts and deposition
368.place: Neuschwanstein, Linderhof and Herrenchiemsee, Bavaria, Germany
368.event: King Ludwig II of Bavaria poured vast sums into fantastic palaces, including Linderhof, Herrenchiemsee, modelled on Versailles, and the fairy-tale castle of Neuschwanstein. Although heavily in debt, he kept on building, and from 1885 foreign banks threatened to seize his property. In June 1886 the Bavarian government had him declared unfit to rule and deposed him, a step not provided for in the Bavarian constitution, and his uncle Luitpold became regent.
368.explanation: Each new project led to more debt and more conflict with his ministers, until the king lost his throne and his castles were opened to paying visitors.
368.tie_back: The kural says that where desire exists, sorrow follows without fail, one upon another, and Ludwig's unending building brought a chain of debts, crises and finally the loss of his crown.
368._accuracy_note: A clear chain of troubles flowing from an insatiable passion, though the medical and political circumstances of his deposition remain debated.

369.event_title: Thoreau's two years at Walden Pond
369.place: Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts, United States
369.event: On 4 July 1845 Henry David Thoreau moved into a small cabin he had built on land owned by Ralph Waldo Emerson beside Walden Pond, where he lived until September 1847. He strictly limited his spending and possessions to test how simply and cheaply a person could live, while writing and studying nature. His account of the experiment, Walden; or, Life in the Woods, was published in 1854 and became a classic of American literature.
369.explanation: Thoreau set out to show that cutting wants down to essentials left more time and freedom for what made life worth living.
369.tie_back: The kural promises that when desire, the sorrow of sorrows, is removed, joy flows unbroken even in this life, and Thoreau's Walden is a famous record of finding contentment by needing less.
369._accuracy_note: A well-known experiment in reducing wants for the sake of a fuller life, though it lasted two years and Thoreau kept close ties to town, so it is not total freedom from desire.

370.event: In the 1970s Bhutan's fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, coined the term Gross National Happiness and asserted that it mattered more than measures of economic output such as gross national or domestic product. Bhutan's development plans have since been guided by this idea, which weighs material growth alongside wellbeing, culture and the environment. The government later developed a Gross National Happiness Index to measure it.
370.explanation: Bhutan made it national policy that endless growth in output is not the goal, setting a lasting kind of wellbeing above ever-rising consumption.
370.tie_back: The kural says desire by its nature can never be satisfied and that lasting contentment comes only when it is set aside, an idea Bhutan applied to a whole economy by refusing to make ever-greater output its highest aim.
370._accuracy_note: Only a loose national-scale analogy to a kural about personal renunciation; sources also differ on the exact year and wording of the king's statement.
